description: We’re a group of students taking part in NASA Space Apps to explore new ideas and learn by building something together. For the Space Mission Design Game challenge, we want to create an engaging game that lets players make mission decisions and see how their choices shape the outcome. We welcome people with different backgrounds and experience levels who are interested in game design...
summary:
Our project is a browser game that lets students aged 10 to 15 run a Moon or Mars outpost for 25 sols. Each sol, players split eight effort points between power, oxygen, food production and radiation shielding. Every point given to one system is taken from another, so students experience the engineering trade-offs that decide whether a mission succeeds or fails.

The game answers the challenge by making these trade-offs tangible and fun. Lunar nights and Martian dust storms cut solar power, while solar flares raise the radiation dose. The flare events are grounded in real data from NASA's DONKI database (CCMC, NASA Goddard): 24 flares were recorded between 1 October and 14 November 2026, including an M6.7 flare on 8 October. Dose values are simplified for gameplay and clearly labelled as such.

It matters because space STEM content often oversimplifies engineering or feels too complex for young learners. Our game teaches systems thinking, risk management and space weather through play, and it runs for free in any browser.
details:
WHAT IT IS ?

Astro Outpost is a free, browser-based game in which students aged 10 to 15 run a Moon or Mars outpost with a crew of four for 25 sols (days). It works on phones and computers, with no installation or account.

HOW IT WORKS ?

Each sol, the player splits 8 effort points between four systems: power, oxygen recycling, food production and radiation shielding. Points given to one system are taken from the others, so every decision has a cost. The player then ends the sol and sees a daily report showing how battery, oxygen, food and radiation dose changed. The mission fails if oxygen or food reaches zero, or if the crew's radiation dose passes the limit. It succeeds if the crew survives 30 sols. The final score depends on resources left and dose received.

Environmental events force trade-offs: lunar nights and Martian dust storms cut solar power, so players must charge the battery in advance, and solar flares raise radiation, so players must raise shielding at the right time. Warnings appear one sol before a flare.

REAL NASA DATA

The flare events come from NASA's DONKI database (CCMC, NASA Goddard). We retrieved 24 solar flares recorded between 1 October and 14 November 2026, including an M6.7 flare on 8 October. The game uses real flares from 5, 6 and 8 October, labelled "Real data · DONKI". One later flare is a clearly marked scenario. Base radiation levels use approximate published surface values for the Moon and Mars. Dose per flare, the dose limit and all resource formulas are game simplifications, not NASA measurements, and the game says so.

BENEFITS AND EXPECTED IMPACT

Students learn that no system can be maximised without hurting another. The game teaches systems thinking, risk management and space weather through play, and it is free, in English and French, and playable on any phone. Teachers can use it in a classroom without setup.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a quiz, the learning happens through consequences: a student who ignores a flare warning sees the dose limit reached. Real flare events from DONKI are replayed inside the game and labelled as real data, so students see that space weather is a real operational risk.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We kept the game accessible for young learners (simple rules, touch-friendly buttons, readable on 360 px screens). We separated the game engine from the interface and tested it. We were transparent about what is real NASA data and what is simplified, and we avoided any NASA branding.

TOOLS

JavaScript, Vite, Vitest (unit tests on a separate game engine), ESLint, Python (data exploration), GitHub and Netlify.

AI USE

AI tools (Claude and Codex) helped us write and refactor code, and draft text. The game rules, the data choices and the testing were directed and checked by our team. No NASA logos or branding are used.
